summary: Documents extensions to RADIUS, already in use in network access server products, that let a server change a user's session while it runs. This includes disconnecting users and changing their authorizations. It replaces RFC 3576. It is informational because it describes deployed behavior rather than a standards-track design.

plainLanguage.summary: RADIUS is how a network asks a server whether a user may log in. This document adds the reverse direction: a way for the server to tell the network to hang up on a user or to change what that user is allowed to do, while the session is still running.

subtitle: How an authentication server can kick a user offline or change what a user is allowed to do, without waiting for the access device to ask.

tldr.problem: Plain RADIUS only lets the access server ask the authentication server questions, so there was no standard way for the server to end a session or change a user's authorization while it was running.
tldr.mechanism: Two extra commands sent to UDP port 3799 let an authorized client ask the access server to disconnect a session or to change its authorization, with an acknowledgement or negative acknowledgement in reply.
tldr.outcome: The extension became a widely deployed way to enforce policy changes on live sessions; RFC 5176 is Informational and documents known limitations that could not be fixed without breaking implementations, and it was later updated by RFC 8559 and RFC 9765.

sections.title: The Missing Direction
sections.content:
The RADIUS protocol does not support unsolicited messages sent from the RADIUS server to the network access server. Yet there are many times when it is desirable to change a session without the access server starting the exchange, such as when an administrator needs to end a session in progress, or when a user changes authorization level and the attributes attached to the session must be added or removed.

To work around this, several vendors added extra RADIUS commands that let the server send unsolicited messages to the access server. These cover Disconnect packets, which end a user session immediately, and Change-of-Authorization packets, which modify session attributes such as data filters.

The document is published as Informational rather than as a standard because of problems that cannot be fixed without breaking deployed implementations, including security weaknesses and a semantic ambiguity in the Change-of-Authorization design. Fixes are recommended but cannot be made mandatory for that reason.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the network asks the server. This extension lets the server also tell the network to end a session or to change a user's permissions, and it is kept as guidance rather than a strict standard because real products already behave in ways that cannot be changed.

sections.title: Disconnect and Change-of-Authorization
sections.content:
A Disconnect-Request is sent by the dynamic authorization client to terminate one or more user sessions on the access server and discard all associated session context. It goes to UDP port 3799 and identifies the access server together with the sessions to be terminated. The access server answers with a Disconnect-ACK if all the session context is discarded and the sessions are gone, or a Disconnect-NAK if it could not disconnect one or more sessions. A Disconnect-ACK may carry an accounting terminate cause of administrative reset.

A Change-of-Authorization request, called a CoA-Request, carries information for dynamically changing session authorizations, most often to change data filters. Ingress or egress filter lists can be sent alongside the identification attributes, using the filter identity or network access server filter rule attributes. It uses the same port and the same packet format as a Disconnect-Request. The access server answers with a CoA-ACK when it can make the change and a CoA-NAK when it cannot.

The packet format has the same Code, Identifier, Length, Authenticator and attribute fields as a normal RADIUS packet, and the request authenticator is computed in the same way as for an accounting request, because there is no user password in these packets. The six decimal codes assigned to the extension are 40 through 45, covering the Disconnect and CoA requests, acknowledgements and negative acknowledgements. The client is responsible for retransmitting requests that get no reply; a retransmission with identical content keeps the same identifier and authenticator, while any change in attributes means a new identifier and authenticator.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two commands: one says hang up on this user, the other says change this user's permissions. Both go to the same special port, and the access device answers with a yes or a no.

sections.title: Identifying the Session
sections.content:
Before an access server can act on a request it has to find the right session. Some attributes identify the access server, such as its IPv4 address, its identifier string, or its IPv6 address. Others identify the session, such as the user name, the port, the framed addresses, the calling and called station identifiers, the accounting session identifier, the multi-session identifier, the port identifier, and the chargeable user identity. The combination must match at least one session, and when it matches several, the request applies to all of them.

Because a privacy network access identifier may hide the real user name, either the user name or the chargeable user identity should be present, and because translation to and from Diameter is easier when the accounting session identifier is known, that attribute should be present too. An access server implementing this specification should send an accounting session or multi-session identifier inside its access requests so the dynamic authorization client knows how to target the session; without it, the client may not be able to single out one session among several.

A Disconnect-Request must contain only access server and session identification attributes; any other attribute causes a negative acknowledgement, optionally with an error cause of unsupported attribute. When a request fails, an Error-Cause attribute gives more detail. Its values divide into ranges: 200 to 299 for success, 400 to 499 for faults committed by the client, and 500 to 599 for faults on the server. Typical values include unsupported attribute, missing attribute, access server identification mismatch, invalid request, unsupported service, session context not found, session context not removable, and multiple session selection unsupported.
sections.plainLanguage: The request must say which device and which session it means, and the answer explains why a request was refused using a numbered cause. A good client keeps the session identifier from accounting so it can point at exactly one session.

sections.title: Proxy State, Authorize Only and Integrity
sections.content:
RADIUS proxies pass along attributes they do not understand. A request may carry Proxy-State attributes, and the access server must return them unchanged in its response. A proxy that adds its own Proxy-State attribute must add it after any existing ones and must not change the order of attributes of the same type; it must remove its own attribute again when the response comes back, and because removing it invalidates the packet's integrity check, the proxy must recompute that check.

To make translation between RADIUS and Diameter easier, a client may include a service type attribute with the value Authorize Only in a CoA-Request. Support for this is optional. Such a request must contain only identification attributes plus a state attribute, and an access server must answer it with a CoA-NAK, not a CoA-ACK; when it succeeds, the negative acknowledgement carries the Authorize Only service type and an error cause of request initiated, after which the access server sends a fresh access request to the RADIUS server to re-authorize the session. A service type attribute must never appear in a Disconnect-Request. The state attribute is otherwise sent by the client and returned unmodified by the access server.

The Message-Authenticator attribute may be used to authenticate and integrity-protect the requests and responses and so prevent spoofing. It is computed with a keyed hash over the type, identifier, length, request authenticator and attributes. A receiver that finds this attribute present but not matching must silently discard the packet. The shared secret between client and server should be at least as large and unguessable as a well chosen password, and the server must use the source IP address of the packet to decide which shared secret applies, so that requests can be proxied.
sections.plainLanguage: Relays that pass the message along must not disturb the bookkeeping stamps that earlier relays added. An optional Authorize Only form asks the server to re-check the user through a normal authorization exchange, and an extra signature can prove the message was not forged.

sections.title: Diameter Considerations
sections.content:
Diameter, the successor protocol, handles server-initiated changes in a different way, so a gateway between the two may find some messages hard or impossible to translate. A Diameter re-authorization request that asks for both authorization and re-authentication cannot be translated directly into a CoA-Request, because a CoA-Request only begins an authorization change, not a re-authentication. A gateway receiving a CoA-Request with authorization changes must instead perform two Diameter exchanges: first a re-authorization request, then a response to the resulting access request carrying the new authorization attributes.

To make this work, the CoA-Request should carry the accounting session identifier, which the gateway can copy into the Diameter session identifier when the Diameter client uses one identifier for both authorization and accounting; otherwise it must map the value across. When the accounting session identifier is absent and the gateway cannot work out the mapping, it can send a negative acknowledgement, possibly with the error cause that multiple session selection is unsupported.

Diameter can also ask for a session to be aborted, and that maps to a Disconnect-Request carrying the accounting session identifier and user name. The document also gives a table that maps each RADIUS error cause to the corresponding Diameter result code, so a gateway can carry the reason for a failure across the two protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Diameter solves the same problem in a cleaner way, so a gateway between the two protocols has to do a little work to translate. Keeping the accounting session identifier in the request makes that translation possible.

sections.title: Authorization, IPsec and Replay
sections.content:
Where several providers share one access server, it would be wrong for one provider to disconnect or change the authorizations of another provider's users. An access server must silently discard requests from untrusted sources. Where a proxy sits between them, it may perform a reverse path forwarding check to confirm that a request comes from an authorized client: it uses the session identification attributes to work out which RADIUS servers an equivalent access request would go to, and forwards the request only if its source address is in that set. Otherwise the request must be silently discarded. Because authorization depends on the source address and the matching shared secret, the server should configure a different shared secret for each client.

Existing implementations use per-packet authentication and integrity algorithms with known weaknesses, so it is recommended that IPsec be used instead, following the RADIUS over IPsec profile. For a server, the policy would require IPsec from any source to the server on UDP port 3799, or a finer rule that requires it only from clients that support IPsec. For a client, the policy would initiate IPsec to any server on that port, or only to servers known to support it.

Existing implementations lack replay protection. Where IPsec replay protection is not used, an Event-Timestamp attribute should be included in requests, and it may be included in responses. When it is present, both sides must check that it is current within an acceptable time window and silently discard the packet otherwise, which requires loose time synchronization. Implementations should be configurable to reject requests that lack the attribute. Because the identifier cannot repeat within the time window, no more than 256 requests can be accepted in that window, so the window must be chosen to match the expected volume; a default of 300 seconds should be adequate in many cases.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted sources may send these commands, and each gets its own secret. The built-in protection is weak, so encryption between the parties is recommended, and a timestamp is used to stop an old message from being replayed.
